I am getting very tired of these sites with the pop-unders and the hijacked back button.

This redundant article by the same crowd (with the same pop-unders and back button hijacking) completely misses the voat.

  1. Removing unofficial flag from government properties does not deny the wonderful and necessary hate speech that we seem to treasure so dearly.

  2. Keeping flag on government buildings actively supports and promotes "hate" or whatever that unofficial flag may seem to stand for.

  3. Corporations -- Amazon, iTunes, Walmart -- that want to censor what we can sell or see are the actual ones blocking free speech.

  4. Article makes no mention of corporate censorship.

Sorry, didn't realize the Washington Times had pop-unders or hijacked the back button. I use Ad Block because of obnoxious Ads like you encountered.

I agree that government buildings should not be flying any flag other than their flag and the flag(s) of 'superior' government entities, e.g. US Flag on a state building. The government has no role in promoting or recognizing any other beliefs.

Private individuals and corporations are free to sell or support whatever they wish. Having said that the political correctness infecting this country is getting old -- particularly when it reaches absurd levels like de-licensing 'Dukes of Hazard' stuff (a show I never liked) and editing 'Gone With the Wind'. What's next banning 'To Kill a Mockingbird'?

It is sad that Disney refuses to distribute 'Song of the South' a wonderful movie full of marvelous folk tales. Unfortunately it is set in the antebellum South where people were treated they should not have been. It is an unfortunate part of our history. Hiding it does not make it less so. Perhaps it is that we're afraid African American folk tales might unduly influence impressionable young minds?

Private individuals and corporations are free to sell or support whatever they wish.

This is the problem here. A company the size of Amazon can significantly reduce "free speech" when it makes editorial decisions. Amazon should be regulated where appropriate. I absolutely do not support general and ideological statements about being "free to sell or support whatever they wish" -- especially where free speech suffers. We can look at concepts and details and make individual decisions based on various circumstances and comparative or competing "values."

Seems to me the only real issue with regard to the Confederate flag is whether it is a state sanctioned symbol, and if it is it is fair to presume the state sanctions all that the symbol represents -- much like the word 'God' on our currency.

As to private individuals and corporations, it is preferable to know where they stand. Knowing that Amazon censors merchandise makes me less likely to patronize them. Do I really want an 'edited' copy of 'Gone With the Wind'? Fortunately, we live in a time when it is easy to find alternative vendors, even for the 'big' guys like Amazon and Walmart. Sometimes that even means ordering something from overseas (like a Philip Pullman book) to get an unadulterated copy.

It doesn't make sense to me why anyone would want to 'require' someone to do business with them. If an individual is so intolerant that they would rather not do business with ____, why would ____ people want to do business with them thereby supporting the very intolerance they decry? One would expect the tolerance would want to avoid doing business with the intolerant. Of course then we get people trying to outlaw intolerance of intolerance.

BTW, I appreciate the tone of this discussion. Kudos flyawayhigh.

Fortunately, we live in a time when it is easy to find alternative vendors, even for the 'big' guys

Generally speaking, the opposite is true. There may be exceptions and you can come up with examples, but the big numbers tell us the opposite. Fewer have greater control of resources and fewer have greater control of transactions.

If Amazon has everything we could possibly want, we have accounts, we've used it, it is reliable, etc., then we go to Amazon. We may never even know of the censorship issue at all -- the issue of censorship itself is censored. Things don't magically pop into our minds. As the saying goes, garbage in, garbage out.

Now, assuming we become aware of the issue as we are in this case, thousands to millions of us can go through all the extra work, the inconvenience, and assume the risk of going somewhere else -- or Amazon can simply be regulated. A simple rule for an internet business with a general used items market is -- trade in all goods, let all comers participate. The large company and its experts can do that easily. The masses of individuals cannot get around it easily. That's the function of regulation.

So, let's say some percentage of the people who oppose Amazon's current censorship go somewhere else. Are they going to get the same prices? Are they going to be able to find everything Amazon sells? How many different places and accounts will they have to open? How much time are they going to spend? What happens when Amazon buys the companies they went to for the purpose of avoiding Amazon? What happens when other companies in the field adopt the same censorship polices? Do you really think that a confederate flag censorship group is going to make a dent in Amazon's business? Isn't it more likely, in fact, pretty much the rule that these large companies get larger and larger?

ALL THIS put upon millions of people versus a regulation upon Amazon.

Capt. Julius Dusenberg raises the Confederate Navy Jack over Shuri Castle on Okinawa after its capture by A Company, Red Battalion of the 5th Marine Regiment on May 29, 1945 [511x666]

On May 29, 1945, A Company, Red Battalion, 5th Marine Regiment, commanded by Capt. Julius Dusenberg, approached to within 800 yards of Shuri Castle. The castle lay within the zone of the 77th Infantry Division, known as the Statue of Liberty Boys. However, General Ushijima’s rear guard had stalled the 77th’s advance. Impatient, Major General del Valle ordered Capt. Dusenberg to “take that … place if you can. I’ll make the explanations.”

Dusenberg’s Marines stormed the stone fortress, quickly dispatching a detachment of Japanese soldiers who had remained behind. Once the castle had been taken, Dusenberg took off his helmet and removed a flag he had been carrying for just such a special occasion. He raised the flag at the highest point of the castle and let loose with a rebel yell. The flag waving overhead was not the Stars and Stripes, but rather the Confederate Navy Jack.

Most of the Marines joined in the yell, but a disapproving New Englander supposedly remarked, “What does he want now? Should we sing ‘Dixie’?” Major General Andrew Bruce, the commanding general of the 77th Division, protested to the 10th Army that the Marines had stolen his prize. But Lieutenant General Buckner only mildly chided General del Valle, saying, “How can I be sore at him? My father fought under that flag!” General Buckner’s father was the Confederate General by the same name!

The Buckner who had surrendered Fort Donelson to General; Ulysses S. Grant in 1862! The flag flew only two days over Shuri Castle, when it was formally raised on May 31, 1945. Dusenberg’s flag was first lowered and presented to General Buckner as a souvenir. General Buckner remarked, “OK! Now, let’s get on with the war!” Tragically, just days before Okinawa fell, General Buckner was killed by an enemy shell on June 18, 1945, on Mezido Ridge, while observing a Marine attack."

Source: http://www.confederatelegion.com/Okinawa.html
